name: Glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline

card.summary: A collagen-derived tripeptide found in supplements; absorbed in animals, with no human skin trials of the peptide itself.
card.note: Evidence for appearance use is essentially absent for the isolated peptide.

quick.overview:
Gly-Pro-Hyp is one of the small peptides produced when collagen is broken down into the hydrolysates sold as supplements.

Research so far covers how it is measured in products and how collagen hydrolysate is absorbed in rats. Human skin studies of the isolated tripeptide were not found.
quick.mechanism: After oral intake, hydrolysates are reported in rats to enter the blood partly as intact peptides. Whether this changes skin in people is the claim made for supplements, and it is not shown for this peptide alone.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to the isolated tripeptide were found. It is not a regulated drug.

lead: Glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline (Gly-Pro-Hyp) is a tripeptide of glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, a sequence characteristic of collagen. It is found in the collagen hydrolysates used in oral collagen supplements and some cosmetic products, which people take with the aim of firmer, smoother, better-hydrated skin; it is one of several small peptides studied as a bioactive component of those preparations.[1][2]

Research on the tripeptide covers how it is measured in products and how it is absorbed. In rats given radiolabelled preparations, a low-molecular-weight collagen hydrolysate was absorbed into the blood in peptide form, Gly-Pro-Hyp remained in plasma and accumulated in the kidney, and radioactivity stayed at a high level in the skin for up to 14 days.[1] A 2024 analytical study developed a mass spectrometry method to quantify Gly-Pro-Hyp and two other peptides in commercial hydrolysates.[2]

In people, trials of skin appearance have tested specific collagen peptide products rather than the isolated tripeptide. A 2014 randomised, placebo-controlled trial of 114 women aged 45 to 65 reported about 20 percent lower eye wrinkle volume after eight weeks of a collagen peptide supplement, with higher procollagen I and elastin in skin biopsies.[3]

chain: Collagen hydrolysate is taken orally or applied
Small peptides such as Gly-Pro-Hyp are absorbed into the blood and reach skin
Peptides are proposed to prompt collagen and elastin production in skin
angle.text: Gly-Pro-Hyp is one of the collagen-derived peptides present in supplements taken for skin appearance. Rat work shows it enters the bloodstream and the label persists in skin, and trials of collagen peptide products have reported fewer eye wrinkles, but the isolated tripeptide has not been tested for skin in people.

paras: Collagen hydrolysates contain bioactive dipeptides and tripeptides, among them Gly-Pro-Hyp. A 2024 analytical study developed a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry method to quantify three such peptides, including Gly-Pro-Hyp, in commercial hydrolysates, reflecting their use in health, cosmetic and therapeutic products.[2] Glycine, proline and hydroxyproline together make up about half of the amino acids in gelatin and hydrolysed collagen, according to Wikipedia.[4]

In rats given radiolabelled preparations, a low-molecular-weight collagen hydrolysate raised plasma radioactivity quickly and was reported to be absorbed into the blood in peptide form, with the Gly-Pro-Hyp label used as one tracer. The tripeptide remained in plasma and accumulated in the kidney, and radioactivity was retained at a high level in the skin until 14 days after administration. That study also examined effects on osteoporosis in the animals.[1]

sections.h: Skin appearance and collagen peptide products
paras: A 2014 double-blind trial in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology gave 114 women aged 45 to 65 either 2.5 g per day of a branded bioactive collagen peptide product or placebo for eight weeks. Eye wrinkle volume was about 20 percent lower than placebo at week 8 and the difference persisted four weeks after stopping; skin biopsies showed higher procollagen I (about 65 percent) and elastin (about 18 percent).[3] The product tested is a specific peptide mixture, and the paper does not attribute the effect to Gly-Pro-Hyp alone.

No safety data specific to the isolated tripeptide were found. Wikipedia notes that hydrolysed collagen is made from meat-industry by-products, and describes regulatory reviews of BSE risk from gelatin in the EU and the US.[4]

No studies found of the isolated Gly-Pro-Hyp tripeptide in people. A 2014 randomised trial tested a collagen peptide mixture for wrinkles; animal and analytical work covers the tripeptide itself.[1][2][3]

timeline.event: Rat study reports absorption of collagen hydrolysate in peptide form, using a Gly-Pro-Hyp tracer.[1]
Randomised trial of a collagen peptide product reports reduced eye wrinkle volume.[3]
LC-MS/MS method developed to quantify Gly-Pro-Hyp in hydrolysates.[2]
